reasoning: Both outputs are strong discovery sessions that refuse to write a PRD, both push back on 'weekly digest email' as a solution masquerading as a problem, and both land on PRD readiness 3/10 with an honest stress test. A wins on a modest but real margin for three reasons. (1) Expectation 3 is answered head-on: A's section 3 is a dedicated falsifiable table of five conditions, each with a 'cheapest check' and a status column marking three as 'Unknown - blocking', then reads the table out loud ('three blockers, all answerable from data you already have, none requiring a build'). B surfaces equivalent material but scatters it across Q2, the break-even formula and a blocking-questions list in section 9, which is less directly the artifact the prompt was asking for. (2) Expectation 4 - A holds the discovery line more consistently. B writes user stories (section 4) for all three jobs and a four-phase v1/v1.1/v1.2/v2 roadmap (section 6), which is PRD-shaped content produced before the fork B itself calls 'the single most valuable thing this session can do'. That is an internal inconsistency and a drift toward the exact polish the eval warns about, even though B never hides the open question. B also closes with a skill-improvement appendix that is off-task for the prompt. (3) Accuracy and sourcing. A cites Google's own sender-guidelines page and dates the Microsoft enforcement change specifically; B's comparable claims rest entirely on vendor blogs and overreach - it attributes a 0.30% complaint ceiling to 'Gmail, Yahoo, Microsoft and Apple' and asserts outright rejection 'since November 2025' with only secondary sourcing. B is not far behind and has genuine advantages: the J1/J2/J3 split is a sharper reframe than A's single solo-vs-multiplayer fork; Option B ('batch the per-event emails you already send', turning this from adding email into reducing it) is a real insight A lacks; the Slack/Teams variant and the one-day signal-density check ('would a teammate want to know this on Friday? under ~20% and it's a ranking problem, not an email problem') are both excellent. But A matches that depth with its own moves - the 'weekly' and 'email' deconstruction, the build-shape cost table showing the event log is the hidden 80%, the branch table in section 9, and the two-hour checkbox pre-probe that is the cheapest signal in either document - while staying tighter to the task.

strengths: Dedicated 'what would have to be true' table (section 3) - five falsifiable conditions, each with the cheapest check and a blocking/resolvable status, then an explicit read of the table as the argument against writing a PRD today
Deconstructs the three decisions smuggled into the one-line request - artifact, cadence, channel - and argues cadence is an output of the change-rate data, not an input to the design
The solo-vs-multiplayer fork is framed as a single query that decides the feature's value, with an explicit 'if solo, don't build it, build here's-where-you-left-off' branch

Build-shape cost table (query-on-send vs event log vs hybrid) makes the point that the email is the last 20% and the event modelling is the project - with the discipline note 'do not let this become we need an event bus first'
Two-hour checkbox pre-probe is the cheapest signal in either document, and it is honest about labelling it 'coming soon' rather than faking a live feature
Sourcing is primary where it matters - Google's own sender guidelines page for the 0.3%/0.1% thresholds, dated Microsoft enforcement change
Explicitly refuses to manufacture TAM/SAM/SOM for a notification feature, and refuses to import benchmark numbers as targets
Stress test concedes the strongest counter-argument ('you've made a two-week feature sound like a research programme') and names the condition under which shipping behind a flag beats the probe
weaknesses: Organises nearly everything around one axis (multiplayer vs solo) and admits in the stress test it invented that frame without knowing the product
Prices fewer delivery alternatives - in-app feed, Slack, badge are named in section 0 but never costed against email the way B costs them
Misses the 'batch the per-event emails you already send' reframe, which would have reduced rather than added email volume
Long; the branch table and synthesis checkpoint restate material already covered

strengths: The J1/J2/J3 table is the sharpest single reframe in either document - one feature name covering three incompatible features with different recipients, content models, metrics and revenue lines - and it names the pick as the blocking decision

Option B in the architecture table ('roll up the per-event emails you already send') flips the feature from adding email to reducing it, changing the risk profile entirely - a real insight A does not have

The one-day signal-density check (query 4 weeks of activity for 10 accounts, ask item by item 'would a teammate want to know this on Friday?', stop under ~20%) is a genuinely cheap, decisive test placed before the probe
Pre-registered build/pivot/kill criteria with explicit numbers, and the reason for a 3-week minimum (a single send measures novelty)
The CAN-SPAM classification trap - the first promotional line in the digest flips it into commercial mail - is a specific, non-boilerplate regulatory catch
Applies the scope-creep discipline to its own session, counting the 9 items it introduced beyond the user's framing
Stress test explicitly downgrades its own deliverability argument as scale-dependent and flags the J3 recommendation as its least-evidenced claim
weaknesses: Writes user stories (section 4) and a four-phase v1/v1.1/v1.2/v2 roadmap (section 6) before the J1/J2/J3 pick it calls the session's most valuable output - PRD-shaped polish produced on top of an unresolved fork, which cuts against its own argument
All regulatory claims rest on vendor blogs; no primary source (no Google/Yahoo/Microsoft sender-guidelines page) despite the claims being load-bearing
Attributes a 0.30% spam-complaint ceiling to 'Gmail, Yahoo, Microsoft and Apple' and asserts outright rejection 'since November 2025' more confidently than the cited secondary sources support
The headline recommendation ('J3 is the one I'd build') is self-labelled low confidence and rests on an unverified prior that the stakeholder variant is under-served
The closing skill-improvement section is off-task for the prompt - useful meta-commentary, but it is not part of answering whether the digest is worth building
